name: Insulin (intravenous)
high_alert_note: Named among the FDA infusion pump page's examples of high-risk infusions; the local high-alert list governs.
summary: Short-acting human insulin product for intravenous use to improve glycaemic control in adults and children with diabetes. The label read is a specific premixed intravenous product; other insulin products differ. Nursing focus: hypoglycaemia, hypokalaemia and glucose monitoring.
evidence_type_note: The evidence here is a regulator product label (prescribing information written for prescribers and pharmacists). It is not a bedside nursing practice guideline: the nursing actions are inferences from label warnings, marked partial, and the unit's protocol governs practice. Guideline-based monitoring statements added in Phase 9 come from UK national guidelines (UKKA July 2026 and JBDS January 2020), read in part only, for adults in UK hospitals; they are marked partial and do not replace the unit's protocol.
jurisdiction_note: US FDA label only. EMA, MHRA and SFDA labels were not read; indications, warnings and presentations differ by country and by manufacturer.

sources.use: regulator label sections (boxed warning, indications, warnings, adverse reactions) read in full text
FDA infusion pump page (high-risk infusion examples)
UKKA acute hyperkalaemia guideline (July 2026): glucose and potassium monitoring after insulin-glucose
JBDS inpatient hypoglycaemia guideline (January 2020): treat as an emergency, do not omit later insulin without review

items.text: The label read describes a short-acting human insulin indicated to improve glycaemic control in adults and paediatric patients with diabetes mellitus; it is a product-specific intravenous label and other insulin products differ.
Changes in insulin regimen should be made under close medical supervision with more frequent blood glucose monitoring.
Monitor potassium levels and treat if indicated, and increase the frequency of blood glucose monitoring in patients at higher risk of hypoglycaemia.
The label calls for monitoring of potassium levels and treating them if indicated.
Hypoglycaemia may be life-threatening; risk is increased by changes in nutrition, co-administered medicines and renal or hepatic impairment.
Severe, life-threatening hypersensitivity, including anaphylaxis, can occur; discontinue, monitor and treat if indicated (a prescriber decision).
Changes in insulin strength, manufacturer, type or method of administration may affect glycaemic control.
The label lists hypoglycaemia, hypersensitivity reactions and hypokalaemia among the adverse reactions discussed in its warnings.

The label also describes peripheral oedema and weight gain with insulin therapy (attributed to sodium retention and the anabolic effects of insulin), and notes that rapid glucose-control intensification has been associated with a transient, reversible eye-refraction disorder and acute painful peripheral neuropathy.
Escalate immediately for low or rapidly falling glucose, low potassium, signs of allergy or any product mix-up.

Use the unit's early warning score (for example, the Royal College of Physicians' NEWS2 track-and-trigger system) to standardise recognition of acute deterioration: a medium aggregate score is a key trigger for an urgent clinical review, and a high aggregate score triggers an emergency clinical response. This is a generic nursing escalation framework, not specific to this medicine; it does not replace this medicine's own escalation triggers, which remain local protocol.
Record glucose and potassium results, pump checks, second-person checks and escalation per unit standard.
Institution-specific preparation: follow your pharmacy's preparation standard and the product labelling. This library gives no preparation or concentration instructions.
Institution-specific dosing: follow the prescriber's order and your institution's approved protocol. This library gives no dosing instructions.

monitoring.text: Monitor blood glucose at the unit's frequency, more often in higher-risk patients.
Watch for signs of hypoglycaemia and allergy.
Report low glucose, low potassium or allergic signs at once.
Record glucose, potassium and pump checks.

After insulin is given with glucose to lower a high potassium, check blood glucose at regular intervals for at least six hours, longer in patients at high risk of late hypoglycaemia (UKKA, UK adults).
Follow potassium results closely after treatment for a rebound once the first effect wears off (UKKA, UK adults).

Treat a low blood glucose as an emergency whatever the level of consciousness; ask the prescriber to review insulin doses instead of omitting later doses on your own (JBDS 2020, UK adults with diabetes).

gaps: Dosing, glycaemic targets, premixed bag strength and preparation: deliberately not included.
